GIRO 2026 · Matrix completion · 3–7 variables

Correlation matrix completion

Fill missing Pearson correlations with a valid, justified completion that preserves supplied information.

Team members: Tim Harrison, Paul Hewson and Xinbin Xu.

Open explorer ↓Download notebook ↓GitHub ↗
Problem, how and result +

Problem

Traditional matrix routes choose missing ordinary correlations directly, or fill the gaps and repair the matrix. Plausible pairwise values need not form a valid matrix; repair adds choices about the objective and which entries may change. Both validity and modelling judgement need justification. [1]

How

Choose maximum entropy as the completion principle. We illustrate it with a Gaussian model: at fixed variances, maximising its entropy is equivalent to maximising det(R). Then express that determinant in partial-correlation vine coordinates. [2] [5]

Result

The vine factorises det(R) into simple terms (1 − ρe2). In the compatible GIRO example, the known factors are fixed, so each free factor is maximised by a zero partial correlation. Four zero assignments complete the optimisation; reconstruction preserves known inputs and gives a positive definite matrix. [5]

Where this demonstration stops +

The explorer accepts 3–7 variable correlation matrices with arbitrary missing pairs. The displayed process follows pages 3–7 of the GIRO presentation. The slide preset uses the rounded numbers displayed on page 3, so its diagnostics differ slightly from the full-precision notebook preset. General nonchordal completion and singular positive semidefinite solutions are outside scope; a rejection here does not prove that every possible completion is impossible.

A correlation matrix does not establish a true dependence structure, marginal distributions or non-Gaussian tail dependence. Partial correlation is not generally conditional correlation. Only with an additional jointly Gaussian assumption can the three-variable 0.4 partial correlation parameterise the Gaussian conditional copula; the conditional copula and partial copula coincide in that specific model.

Validation is numerical, at stated tolerances, and needs care near singularity. Display values are rounded; checks use full precision. The example has no out-of-sample test or empirical insurance calibration.

Conclusion

Vines expose modelling choices

A partial-correlation vine makes the dependence model visible: which variables connect, what is conditioned on, and which partial correlations are supplied or assumed. Together with the completion principle, these choices shape the completed matrix and can be explained, tested and revised as information changes. The full story [6]

Notes and references +

  1. Information and feasibility

    The inputs are ordinary Pearson correlations. Missing entries need a valid completion and justified modelling choices; supplied entries, including known zeros, stay fixed. The default GIRO example has five variables, six supplied pairs and four missing pairs.

    The traditional matrix routes compared here are direct assignment of missing ordinary correlations and filling a matrix followed by positive-semidefinite repair. Plausible individual entries do not guarantee whole-matrix validity. Repair requires an objective, such as a chosen distance, and decisions about which entries must stay fixed. A constrained direct or repair method can preserve supplied information; the comparison does not assume that every repair changes known entries.

    For a documented comparison of maximum-determinant completion and nearest-correlation repair with specified entries fixed, see Georgescu, Higham & Peters (2017), §§2 and 5. This is an example, not evidence that one filling or repair practice is universal.

    The full-precision notebook preset is separate from the rounded slide preset. Its completed 1–3 covariance is −16.7780, corresponding to an ordinary correlation of −0.4601.

    There are n(n−1)/2 distinct off-diagonal correlations. Supplied pairs are fixed constraints; missing pairs remain to be selected by the completion rule and any modelling judgements. The counts describe available information, not estimation accuracy.

    Apply a valid input to see its feasibility checks.

    For a chordal observed graph, positive definite fully specified maximal blocks (cliques) ensure that a positive definite completion exists. For a nonchordal graph, these block checks alone do not establish feasibility. This explorer’s maximum-determinant solver supports chordal graphs. An unsupported calculation is reported explicitly.

    References: Grone et al. (1984); Kurowicka & Cooke (2006), §4.2.

    Back to the linked text ↑

  2. Regular vine construction, labels and partial correlations

    First tree. T1 has the original n variables as nodes. Connect them with n−1 edges to make one connected tree without cycles.

    Higher trees. The edges of T(k−1) become the nodes of Tk. Each Tk must again be a connected tree without cycles: it has n−k+1 nodes and n−k edges. Continue to T(n−1), which has one edge.

    Proximity rule. From T2 onwards, two nodes may connect only if the edges they represent share a node in the preceding tree. For example, the T1 edges 12 and 24 may connect in T2, giving the label 14;2.

    Judgement 1 selects the structure. Step 2 constructs Greedy, C-vine or D-vine trees automatically, or lets you edit manual connections. Greedy uses known information first, then strongest absolute correlation. At each tree, it prioritises eligible edges whose required input blocks are fully supplied; T1 uses ordinary correlations and higher trees use partial correlations. Stable labels break ties and cycles are avoided. This is a local choice given earlier trees, not a search over complete vines. The connected-tree and proximity rules govern validity; preserving supplied ordinary correlations is a separate completion requirement. These rules do not establish that the modelling choices are appropriate.

    Node set labels retain the paper’s semicolon: the conditioned pair comes first and the conditioning set follows, for example 12;34. The separator is omitted for an empty conditioning set. Coefficients in both graphs and equations use the project’s dot notation, for example ρ12·3,4. Higher-tree nodes represent preceding-tree edges; connections obey proximity.

    A partial correlation concerns linear regression residuals. It is not generally a correlation conditional on a fixed value. Free partial values are modelling judgements in explicit-vine mode and are derived from the selected optimum in maximum-determinant mode. A chosen set can conflict with the supplied correlations.

    Reference: Kurowicka & Cooke (2006), Definitions 3.1–3.2 and §2.1.

  3. Validity, objective and practical scope

    The result reconstructs the missing ordinary correlations. Positive definite implies positive semidefinite. The scenario download records the supplied input, selected structure, partial assignments, completion method, result and calculations so those choices can be reviewed and reproduced.

    The checks establish numerical positive definiteness and preservation of supplied entries. A maximum-determinant certificate concerns that objective under the supplied-entry constraints; it does not show closeness to an unknown true matrix. The Gaussian entropy interpretation additionally needs a Gaussian model and fixed variances.

    Algebraic validity does not justify the assumptions. With further business information, underwriters can help articulate residual dependence for partial-correlation judgements. Such judgements need supporting evidence and review; a partial correlation alone does not specify a copula or tail behaviour.

    Inputs here are illustrative. The demo has no empirical insurance calibration or out-of-sample validation. A correlation matrix alone does not identify marginal distributions, a copula family or tail dependence. The app reports unsupported choices without changing the requested method.

    See Method & sources and Grone et al. (1984) for the determinant criterion.

    Back to the linked text ↑

  4. Generating-reference comparison

    Generated examples keep a full reference matrix separate from solver inputs. The comparison measures agreement with that synthetic reference; the selected objective need not recover it. Editing supplied values may make the original reference incompatible with the current constraints. Hidden reference values are excluded from solver requests.

    Back to the linked text ↑

  5. Maximum entropy → determinant → vine factors

    The maximum-entropy principle selects a model by maximising entropy subject to the stated information. This is the completion principle chosen here; the constraints and admissible model class matter. It does not guarantee the empirically closest result to an unknown true model.

    Gaussianity is our worked example, rather than the definition of maximum entropy. For a Gaussian vector with fixed variances, differential entropy differs from ½ log det(R) by a constant. Maximising Gaussian entropy therefore reduces to maximising det(R), equivalently log det(R), while preserving the supplied correlations. Among feasible positive definite completions this optimum is unique.

    The supplied correlations and fixed variances constrain second moments. Maximum entropy gives a declared baseline when further dependence information is limited. The matrix alone does not establish Gaussianity or validate a model for tails.

    A complete labelled partial-correlation vine gives the determinant identity

    det(R) = ∏e(1 − ρe2).

    Here e ranges over the vine edges: first-tree values are ordinary correlations, and higher-tree values are partial correlations. This factorisation is algebraic; Gaussianity is needed for the entropy interpretation, not for the determinant identity itself.

    In the compatible default GIRO vine, six coordinates are determined by supplied information and four remain free. The determinant becomes a fixed positive factor K times four free factors:

    det(R) = K ∏e ∈ F(1 − ρe2).

    Each free factor is at most one and reaches one at ρe = 0. Thus the optimisation reduces to four zero partial assignments, followed by ordinary-correlation reconstruction. A zero partial correlation can produce a nonzero ordinary correlation.

    This simplification relies on the compatible representation and its fixed known factors. Arbitrary zeros on another vine need not preserve the supplied entries or maximise determinant. Use Maximum determinant to calculate the optimum for the current supported input; changing only the vine representation does not improve that optimum.

    At the optimum, the inverse correlation matrix is zero at unspecified-entry positions. The displayed certificate checks this condition. This implementation computes the chordal solution; changing only the displayed vine representation leaves the optimum unchanged.

    References: Grone et al. (1984); Kurowicka & Cooke (2006), §4.2; Vandenberghe, Boyd & Wu (1998), §§2.2 and 2.6.

    Back to the linked text ↑

  6. How vines expose dependence-modelling choices

    The problem is to complete missing ordinary Pearson correlations while preserving supplied information. Numerical validity is necessary, but it does not tell us which modelling assumptions are justified.

    The comparison here covers direct ordinary-correlation assignment and filling followed by matrix repair, as well as completion through a partial-correlation vine. Bounds on individual ordinary correlations do not ensure that the whole matrix is positive semidefinite. A valid vine provides a structured parameterisation in which partial correlations describe residual linear dependence. Keeping supplied entries also requires compatible inputs and assignments; the software checks both preservation and definiteness.

    Modelling includes the information treated as fixed, the completion principle and distributional assumptions, as well as the vine structure and its free partial-correlation assignments. A vine exposes the connections, conditioning relationships and residual-dependence assumptions within that model. The structural validity rules constrain possible connections; Greedy is a chosen selection heuristic. A partial correlation describes residual linear dependence after accounting for the conditioning variables.

    A direct matrix method can also enforce validity, preserve supplied constraints and maximise determinant. Under the same constraints, changing only the vine representation does not improve that optimum. What the vine route adds is an explicit organisation of conditioning relationships and partial-correlation assumptions that can be explained, tested and revised. These assumptions may come from data, a completion criterion or expert judgement. No comparison of prediction accuracy or computational speed is claimed, and no particular matrix-repair practice is assumed to be standard.

    For the compatible worked GIRO example, Gaussian maximum entropy with fixed variances provides the maximum-determinant baseline and its four free partials are zero. This does not make arbitrary zero assignments universally optimal. Qualification and references [5].

    The resulting positive definite matrix preserves known inputs and completes the missing entries under the selected information, structure and assignments. It need not be closest to an unknown true matrix. With further business information, underwriters can help articulate residual dependence, refine the partial judgements and compare another completion. The tool makes these choices inspectable; it does not supply empirical justification for them.

    For example, with known ρ12 = ρ23 = 0.5, maximum determinant gives ρ13 = 0.25. Choosing the additional partial judgement ρ13·2 = 0.4 instead gives ρ13 = 0.55. The changed ordinary correlation reflects the extra assumption.

    The broader contribution is to make dependence modelling explicit and open to revision. Expert judgement is one input to that process. Recorded model choices, supporting evidence and a reproducible result allow others to inspect the assumptions and assess their consequences. Margins, a copula family and non-Gaussian tail behaviour still require further modelling information.

    See the construction and partial-correlation references [2] and maximum-determinant references [5].
